insights.title: You score more with the Queen's Gambit than with your other White openings
insights.detail: You score 59% in 467 games where your rating predicts 50%: 9 points per 100 games above your rating, while your other 1202 games as White score 1 per 100 above your rating. The gap is 7 points per 100 games (about 52 Elo). It makes up 28% of your games as White.

insights.title: You abandoned 71 games, and each one costs rating points
insights.detail: You abandoned 71 of your 3354 games (your opponents abandoned 114). Each one counts as a full loss and costs rating points in rated games. Going by the ratings you could have expected about 35.0 points from those games.
study: Only start a rated game when you are sure you have time to finish it; play unrated or daily games when you might be interrupted.
Check your connection and battery before a rated session, and play on even in bad positions: opponents at club level often let you back in.

insights.title: You draw 3.2% of your games
insights.detail: You drew 109 of 3354 games (3.2%): 0.8% in bullet, 3.8% in blitz, 5.6% in rapid, 5.7% in daily. The most common kind of draw is by repetition (32 of 109).
study: Replay your draws by repetition and agreement: were any of them in positions where you were better and could have played on?
In equal endgames against lower-rated players, keep playing: most club players go wrong under sustained pressure.

insights.title: Your engine accuracy: 80 in wins, 84 in draws, 72 in losses
insights.detail: Your average engine accuracy (Lichess's formula, 0-100) was 79.6 in 146 wins, 84.4 in 2 draws, 72.3 in 152 losses. Your opponents averaged 75.0 over the same games.
study: Compare your least accurate losses (linked): were they lost to one big blunder or to many small inaccuracies? The fix is different.
In each linked loss, find the first move that lost 10% or more of your winning chances and name what you should have checked.

insights.title: You saved 42 of 133 lost positions (32%)
insights.detail: In 133 games your opponent got a winning position first (you had at most 15% winning chances); you still drew or won 42 of them. Your opponents saved 46 of the 132 games where you got there first (35%).
study: In a lost position, set practical problems: keep pieces on, create threats and make every move matter for your opponent.
Replay the linked comebacks to see which defensive ideas worked for you.

insights.title: You missed 46 forced checkmates (your opponents 59)
insights.detail: Stockfish saw a forced mate for you 46 times that you didn't follow through (your opponents: 59); you also allowed 111 forced mates against you (your opponents: 97).
study: Solve mate-in-2 and mate-in-3 puzzles until the common patterns (back rank, smothered, Anastasia's) are automatic.
When your opponent's king is exposed, look at every check first, even ones that sacrifice material.

insights.title: Queen moves account for 17% of your blunders
insights.detail: Queen moves were 13% of your moves but 17% of your 666 blunders (112). Your blunder rate peaks at moves 11–20 (11.6 per 100 moves).
study: Before every queen move, check which squares and pieces it stops guarding and whether it can be attacked or trapped on its new square.
Keep a blunder log: for each blunder note the piece, the move number and what you missed; patterns repeat.
Around moves 11–20, slow down and double-check every capture and check for both sides.

insights.title: Sicilian Defense, move 5: you played 5...e5 in 10 of 21 games; 5...a6 is better
insights.detail: After 1.e4 c5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Nc3 e6 4.d4 cxd4 5.Nxd4 you played 5...e5 in 10 of the 21 games that reached this position. study: Set up the position after 1.e4 c5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Nc3 e6 4.d4 cxd4 5.Nxd4 and work out why 5...a6 beats 5...e5.
